newsitem.title: USA: CME official criticizes FASB derivatives proposals.
newsitem.headline: CME official criticizes FASB derivatives proposals.

text.p: A Chicago Mercantile Exchange official Tuesday criticized proposed changes in accounting rules for derivatives by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) as "wrongheaded" and unnecessary.
Ira Kawaller, director of the CME's New York office, told a public hearing that the FASB's proposed overhaul would discriminate against certain products traded on the CME.

"The critical area for us is the prohibition relating to the tenor of derivatives, or the requirement that the maturity of the derivative reach and/or exceed the maturity of the underlying exposure," said Kawaller.
He said the FASB proposal would hurt "rollover hedging," and disallow correctly structured tailed hedges, which appropriately offset present values of exposures.

Rollover hedging is used for exposures that will occur at some point in the future. "In practice, you lose a derivative position that will have a shorter life, and then you'll just roll over that position," said Kawaller.

"My biggest concern is that the differential accounting treatment that you're proposing for a rollover hedge versus a more traditional hedge is one that's going to force people to choose a wrong instrument from a business point of view."
Kawaller said the FASB's treatment of hedging was based on comparisons that were simply "wrongheaded."
Kawaller testified on the third day of a four-day public hearing on the FASB's proposals.
The CME is among the two biggest futures exchanges in the U.S. It trades a variety of financial and agricultural futures, including contracts tied to interest rates, livestock and stock indices.
At the hearing, the FASB has heard mostly negative feedback on its proposal to require companies to carry all derivatives on their balance sheets at current market value.

Under current practice, many derivatives -- financial instruments whose value is based on the value of another instrument, asset or market index -- are carried off-balance sheet, and similar transactions may receive disparate accounting treatment.
